_comment: Single source of truth for the project case studies. portfolio-details.html renders every entry from this file, so adding a project means adding an object here and nothing else. Keep 'outcome' honest — leave it null rather than inventing a number.

projects.name: UrbanKart
projects.tagline: MERN e-commerce platform with payments and an admin dashboard
projects.problem: Most tutorial e-commerce builds stop at a product list and a fake checkout. I wanted to build the parts that actually make a store usable: real payments, real sessions, and an admin who can change the catalogue without touching the database.
approach: Split authentication into two roles — customers and admins — behind JWT, with Google OAuth as a second sign-in path so buyers aren't forced to create yet another password.
Built the admin dashboard as a separate route tree with its own guard, so catalogue and order management never share a surface with the storefront.
Integrated Razorpay for payments, verifying the signature server-side rather than trusting the client callback.
Modelled cart state on the server so a cart survives a device change, instead of keeping it only in localStorage.
projects.learned: Signature verification is the whole point of a payment integration — the client callback tells you what the browser claims happened, not what the payment provider recorded. Moving that check server-side was the difference between a demo and something I'd let a real customer use.

projects.name: Pizzeria
projects.tagline: Real-time pizza ordering with live status tracking
projects.problem: An order status page that only updates when you refresh is worse than no status page — the customer refreshes anyway, and the kitchen gets a phone call. The interesting problem was pushing state changes out rather than waiting to be asked.
approach: Kept order status as a single server-side state machine (placed → confirmed → prepared → delivered) so the kitchen dashboard and the customer view can never disagree.
Pushed transitions over a live connection instead of polling, so the customer's page reflects a kitchen action within a second.
Gave the admin dashboard the same event stream the customer gets, so one implementation serves both.
Separated customer and admin sessions so a logged-in customer can't reach kitchen controls by guessing a URL.
projects.learned: Modelling status as an explicit state machine, rather than a string field anyone could write to, removed a whole class of bugs where an order could jump backwards or skip a step.

projects.name: Meta Photos
projects.tagline: Photo and video gallery with cloud-backed uploads
projects.alt: Meta Photos gallery, a Google Photos clone
projects.problem: Storing user-uploaded media on the application server means the first popular user fills the disk, and every deploy risks the files. I wanted to learn how media is actually handled in production.
approach: Handled multipart uploads with Multer, then streamed straight to Cloudinary rather than writing to local disk.
Stored only the returned URLs and metadata in MongoDB, keeping the database small and the app server stateless.
Scoped every query to the owning user so one account's media is never reachable from another's session.
Used server-rendered EJS views to keep the first paint fast on a media-heavy page.
projects.learned: A stateless app server is what makes redeploying safe. Once uploads went to object storage instead of the filesystem, deploys stopped being something to worry about.

projects.name: Live Location Tracker
projects.tagline: Real-time position sharing on an interactive map
projects.problem: Browser geolocation fires far more often than a map needs to redraw, and every update is a network message. Sending all of them makes the map jitter and wastes the connection.
approach: Subscribed to the Geolocation watch API and throttled updates before they reach the socket, rather than emitting on every fix.
Broadcast positions by connection id so a client can render other participants without any of them sharing an account.
Cleaned up markers on disconnect, so a closed tab doesn't leave a ghost pin on everyone else's map.
projects.learned: Throttling at the source is much cheaper than de-duplicating downstream. It also made the map feel calmer, which was a UX win I hadn't expected from a performance change.

projects.name: AUXES IT Solutions
projects.tagline: Company website built and deployed during my time there
projects.alt: Auxes IT Solutions company website homepage
projects.problem: The company needed an official site that non-developers could keep current, and it had to go live on a fixed date around existing client work.
approach: Built the front end and the REST layer behind it, so content changes don't require a redeploy.
Worked to a fixed launch date alongside the team's existing commitments.
Handled the deployment and post-launch fixes myself.
projects.learned: Shipping to someone else's deadline is a different skill from building something well. Scoping honestly at the start mattered more than working faster at the end.
projects.outcome: Recognised internally for clean code practices and on-time delivery.

projects.name: QuickPick
projects.problem: An earlier attempt at a store before UrbanKart — the version where I worked out how catalogue, cart and checkout fit together before rebuilding it properly.
approach: Loaded the product catalogue over an API rather than hardcoding it, so the same front end works against different data.
Built a persistent cart and a checkout flow with payment integration.
Kept the admin upload path separate from the storefront.
projects.learned: Building the same problem twice taught me more than any single project — the second version was better mostly because I already knew which decisions I'd regret.
